nameStory: The meal moth gets its name from its larvae's appetite for milled grains and flour - "meal" being an old term for ground grain products. Even 18th-century naturalists recognized this kitchen invader, giving it scientific names that translate to "of the flour" and "of home and hearth" because it was such a familiar household companion.
description: The meal moth is a small brownish moth with a wingspan of about an inch that you're most likely to encounter fluttering around your pantry or barn. Unlike many moths that hold their wings horizontally, meal moths have a distinctive habit of curling their abdomen tip upward at a right angle to their body when at rest. Their forewings are relatively colorful for a moth, with warm brown and tan patterns that help them blend in among stored grains and farm settings. These quick-breeding moths can produce multiple generations in a single year.

idTips.label: Curved Abdomen Posture
idTips.description: When resting, the moth holds its abdomen tip at a 90-degree angle to its body, creating an unmistakable curved silhouette that no other common household moth displays

idTips.label: Wingspan Size
idTips.description: Small moths with wings spanning roughly three-quarters to just over an inch across - about the size of a large thumbnail

idTips.label: Wing Coloration
idTips.description: Forewings show warm brown and tan patterns that are fairly bright and contrasting for a moth, with distinct markings that catch the light

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a somewhat erratic, fluttery pattern typical of small moths, often attracted to lights in pantries and storage areas

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Almost always found near stored grain products, flour, or animal feed - if you see it in your kitchen or barn, you're likely looking at a meal moth

habitat: In New England, meal moths are most commonly found in human-made environments like barns, grain storage facilities, feed stores, and home pantries where milled grains and flour are stored. They thrive in warehouses and agricultural buildings throughout the region's farming areas, from the Connecticut River Valley to rural Vermont and New Hampshire. You might also spot them around poultry farms and livestock operations where animal feed creates ideal breeding conditions.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging as temperatures warm, starting their breeding cycle in stored grain environments.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season from June through August when adults are most active and visible, especially around artificial lights near storage areas.
seasonality.fall: Late-season generations may still be active in heated buildings and storage facilities as outdoor temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults are rare outdoors but may continue their life cycle in heated barns, feed stores, and homes where grain products are stored.

funFact: In parts of China, meal moths are deliberately cultivated to make "insect tea" - a traditional beverage that's popular enough that scientists are now studying the moths' optimal growing conditions for potential commercial farming!
confusionNotes: Meal moths are often confused with Indian meal moths and other pantry pests, but the meal moth's distinctive habit of curling its abdomen upward at a right angle when resting is a dead giveaway - other pantry moths hold their bodies straight.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "meal" moth, this refers to ground grain meal, not the word meaning a food serving. These moths have been human companions for so long that early naturalists gave them names meaning "brother-like" and "domestic," recognizing them as practically part of the household.
compareHints: The meal moth is the only member of its genus commonly found in New England, making it unique among its immediate relatives. Compared to other pyralid snout moths in the region, meal moths are distinguished by their distinctive resting posture with the curved abdomen and their strong association with stored grain products rather than natural plant materials.
